guidance:
Work strictly within Table 1. Ignore other tables, figures, narrative text, and footnotes as data sources (but you may use them to understand structure).

1) Columns and headers
- First, reconstruct the full header from left to right.
- Collect every explicit data column header into `columns`. This typically includes each group, arm, timepoint, or summary column, and any dedicated column such as an effect size.
- If headers are multi-level (a top header spanning several subheaders), do not add the top header alone as a column. Instead, form a unique label for each leaf by combining them (e.g., "Group: Subheader"). Use that combined label as `column_label` and include it once in `columns`.
- The leftmost label column sometimes has a heading. If it does, include that heading in `columns`, but never create cells for it; its entries are represented in `row_label`.
- Every `column_label` used in any cell must appear exactly once in `columns`; do not invent extra columns or totals.

2) Distinguishing row_group and row_label
- Read the table down the leftmost column and visually separate:
  • Section/category headings (often spanning multiple columns or styled differently).
  • Data rows (aligned with actual values in the data columns).
- A section heading that precedes a block of rows is `row_group`. The text within the section is `row_label` for each row.
- For rows inside a section, set `row_group` to the section heading string and `row_label` to the item name on that row.
- Rows that are not clearly under any heading use `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has data values on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is the broader category; `row_label` is the specific item.

3) Creating cells
- A cell corresponds to a single non-empty intersection of one data row and one data column.
- For every visible numeric or textual entry in the body of Table 1, emit exactly one cell object with four fields: `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, `value`.
- Copy `value` exactly as printed, including spaces, punctuation, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and text such as "N/A" or dashes used as values.
- A printed zero is a real value and must be included.
- Do not emit cells for blank table entries. Never invent or infer values.

4) Avoiding missing and extra cells
- For each row, scan across all data columns and ensure that every non-empty cell is represented once in the output.
- Do not create cells for rows that hold only headers and no data values.
- Do not add aggregate columns that are not explicitly part of the header (e.g., a total derived from visible columns) and do not reassign values to different groups or categories.
- Check that each (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) combination appears at most once; if the table layout causes apparent repetition, confirm whether it is truly a second distinct data entry before adding another cell.

5) Consistency of strings
- Use the table text verbatim for `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, preserving spelling, symbols, and capitalization.
- If the same section or column appears more than once, reuse the exact same string so that rows are correctly grouped.

Apply these steps to every Table 1, including complex layouts, to capture all data faithfully without adding or omitting cells.
